newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy may regain vigor after fall lull.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy may regain vigor after fall lull.

text.p: The economy grew at a slower rate in the third quarter than previously estimated, the government reported Wednesday, but signs of slightly stronger consumer spending bolstered hopes for a solid holiday sales season.

The Commerce Department said gross domestic product, the broadest measure of the nation's economy, grew at a revised 2 percent annual rate in the quarter instead of the 2.2 percent it reported a month ago.
Though less than half the 4.7 percent rate of growth in the second quarter, the revised rate showed the current expansion that began in March 1991 remained intact, analysts said.
"It's not a setback, just a pause on the way to moderate and healthy economic expansion in the fourth quarter and on into 1997," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis.

While most of the overall drop in growth came from slower consumer spending, the department said spending was a bit stronger than estimated a month ago, rising at a 0.6 percent rate, rather than a 0.4 percent rate, in the quarter. Spending had risen at a 3.4 percent rate in the second quarter.

Consumers fuel about two-thirds of the economy through their purchases of goods and services. Typically, half or more of total annual retail sales occur in the few weeks from Thanksgiving through Christmas.
Sohn said he expects the economy will grow at a rate of 3 percent or so in the fourth quarter, largely on a rebound in spending as consumers regain their holiday shopping spirit.
"Christmas sales will be reasonably good because consumers do have jobs, growing incomes, rising confidence and healthy balance sheets due to big stock market gains," Sohn said.
A University of Michigan survey Wednesday showed consumer confidence jumped to 99.2 in November from 96.5 in October, financial market sources who subscribe to the report said.
Meanwhile, the Labour Department reported separately that new applications for jobless pay were steady last week at 342,000, pointing to a largely stable job market.
A separate Commerce Department report pointed to steady if unspectacular growth in manufacturing.
Orders for durable goods edged up 0.1 percent in October to a seasonally adjusted $174.2 billion after a much stronger 4.6 percent September increase, the department said.
The increase came wholly from a record 17.3 percent surge in orders for electrical gear. Orders for new cars, airplanes, primary metals, industrial machinery and defence items all slumped.
Analysts said the industrial sector was chugging along.

"While flat, this report is no turkey," said economist Ken Mayland of KeyCorp in Cleveland, Ohio. "Orders are still exhibiting enough forward momentum to keep the manufacturing sector gainfully occupied at least into early 1997."

A report from the Purchasing Management Association of Chicago appeared to bolster that notion, as its regional index of manufacturing rose to 57.6 in November from 56.9 in October. A reading above 50 signals growth, while one below that suggests contraction.
Orders and production were brisker in November, the group of corporate buyers said, adding its index continued to signal "solid, if unspectacular, growth."

Separately, the Conference Board said its index of help wanted advertising dipped two points to 82.0 in October, a relatively small change that did not imply a rapid slowdown in the job market in coming months.

"The pace of jobs growth will not subside in the early months of 1997," said Ken Goldstein, economist at the New York-based business research group. "Sustained job growth will bolster consumer confidence and lead to stronger consumer spending through the first half of the (new) year."
